mainTopic: Reopening a verdict: a judge's mistakes, retrial rules in capital and related cases, and who may argue
overview: The amud opens by rejecting a reading of the משנה's rule 'מחזירין לזכות ואין מחזירין לחובה' as two kinds of acquittal. The reason is that no one would execute a person for the sake of the גואל הדם, and the wording 'בין... בין' does not fit. רבינא then explains how a judge can cause a loss with his own hands: by taking collateral, by touching an item to a שרץ, or by mixing impure produce into pure produce. Next, a ברייתא learns from 'נקי וצדיק אל תהרג' that in דיני נפשות a case is reopened to acquit but never to convict. For a מסית the rule is reversed. רב ששת extends the retrial rules to חייבי גלות (from 'רוצח') and to חייבי מלקות (from 'רשע'), and a ברייתא supports him. רבי יוחנן limits 'no retrial to convict' to mistakes in matters the צדוקים reject. A mistake in a clear written law, like נואף, is reversed, while a mistake about relations שלא כדרכה is not. Finally, רב פפא explains that the משנה's 'everyone may argue for acquittal' means the students, not the witnesses, so it fits all views.

steps.title: Reading the clause as two kinds of acquittal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that 'they bring back for acquittal' means a plain acquittal. 'They do not bring back for liability' means an acquittal that also causes someone a loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: '...but they do not bring back for liability.' 'They bring back for acquittal' means a plain acquittal. 'They do not bring back for liability' means an acquittal that is also a liability.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the end of the rule about דיני נפשות and offers a new way to read it. On this reading, both halves talk about acquitting, not about convicting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally we read the rule as: you may reverse a ruling to acquit, but not to convict. This suggestion changes that. Both halves are about acquittal. A plain acquittal may be reversed, but an acquittal that causes someone else a loss may not.

keyTerms.meaning: They bring back (reopen or reverse the ruling)
For acquittal, in favor of the accused
For liability, against someone
Plain, alone, with nothing else attached

steps.confusionAlert: Watch out: in this proposed reading, 'לחובה' does NOT mean convicting the accused. It means an acquittal that is a 'חובה' (a loss) for someone else.

phrases.english: but they do not bring back for liability.
'They bring back for acquittal' means a plain acquittal,
'and they do not bring back for liability' means
an acquittal that is a liability.

steps.triggerLanguage: מחזירין לזכות – זכות גרידתא, ואין מחזירין לחובה – לזכות שהיא חובה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion from before this section by offering a new reading of the quoted rule.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'לחובה' means reversing a ruling in order to convict.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both halves deal with acquittal: a plain acquittal, or an acquittal that causes a loss to someone.

steps.title: A loss for whom?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who could lose out from an acquittal in a capital case.
steps.simpleTranslation: A liability for whom?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the new reading by asking who would be hurt by an acquittal in a capital case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a money case there are two sides, so one side's win is the other side's loss. In דיני נפשות there is only the accused and the court, so it is unclear who an acquittal could harm.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose liability? A loss for whom?

phrases.english: A liability for whom?

steps.triggerLanguage: חובתיה דמאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the reading from step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who is the other party who loses from an acquittal in a capital case?

steps.title: The loss is to the גואל הדם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the loss belongs to the גואל הדם, the relative who wants the killer punished.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult: it is a liability for the גואל הדם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names a person who loses out when the accused is acquitted: the גואל הדם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גואל הדם is the victim's relative who wants the killer to die. If the killer is acquitted, the relative loses what he wanted. So an acquittal can be called a 'חובה' for him.

keyTerms.meaning: This is not difficult
The blood redeemer, the victim's close relative who pursues the killer

phrases.english: This is not difficult;
it is the liability of the blood redeemer.

steps.triggerLanguage: הא לא קשיא, חובתיה דגואל הדם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The loss is to the גואל הדם, who wanted the killer put to death.

steps.title: Would we execute someone because of the גואל הדם?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that it makes no sense to refuse to acquit a person, and so put him to death, just to protect the גואל הדם's interest.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of the liability of the גואל הדם, we kill this person?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 3 with a strong question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If there is a good reason to acquit, the court must save the accused. A relative's wish for revenge cannot outweigh a person's life. So the 'חובה of the גואל הדם' cannot be why the court refuses to reverse the ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: We kill, we execute

phrases.english: Because of the liability of the blood redeemer
we kill this one?
phrases.notes: This is a shocked question, meaning: surely not!

steps.triggerLanguage: משום חובתיה דגואל הדם קטלינן ליה להאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the 'חובה' is the גואל הדם's loss
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person's life cannot be given up because a relative wants revenge.

steps.title: The words 'בין... בין' point to two opposite things
steps.stepSummary: A second objection: the source says 'בין לזכות בין לחובה' (whether for acquittal or for liability). That wording describes two separate directions, not two kinds of acquittal.
steps.simpleTranslation: And further, what is the meaning of 'whether' and 'whether'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second problem, this time from the wording of the source itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: About דיני ממונות, the source says the court reverses 'בין לזכות בין לחובה'. 'Whether this or that' clearly means two opposite outcomes: acquitting or convicting. So 'לחובה' must mean real liability, which breaks the reading from step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: And further, introducing another problem
Whether... or, listing two separate options

phrases.english: And further, what is 'whether... whether'?
phrases.notes: He means the money-case line: 'whether for acquittal, whether for liability', which sounds like two opposite things.

steps.triggerLanguage: ועוד, מאי בין בין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second challenge to the reading from step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of 'לחובה' as 'an acquittal that is a liability'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'בין... בין' lists two opposite outcomes, so 'לחובה' must mean real conviction.

steps.title: The reading stays difficult
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the proposed reading remains difficult and is not accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends this line of thought: the problems were not answered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plain 'קשיא' means the challenges stand and the suggestion from step 1 is dropped. The גמרא now needs a different way to explain the earlier question.

keyTerms.meaning: It is difficult; the problem stands unanswered

steps.whatToRemember: The attempt to read 'אין מחזירין לחובה' as 'an acquittal that harms someone' fails. It does not make sense to execute someone for the גואל הדם's sake, and the 'בין... בין' wording does not fit.

phrases.english: It is difficult.

steps.triggerLanguage: קשיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the challenges of steps 4 and 5 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The reading from step 1 is rejected.

steps.title: רבינא: the judge took the collateral away
steps.stepSummary: רבינא gives a new way a judge can cause a loss with his own hands when he wrongly exempts a liable party: he takes the collateral from the lender and hands it over.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: For example, where the lender had collateral in his hand, and the judge took it from him.
steps.whatsHappening: After the rejected reading, רבינא offers a new answer. He explains how a judge who wrongly exempted someone in a money case did the damage himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just declaring someone exempt is only words. But if the lender was holding a משכון and the judge took it away from him, the judge physically moved the item to the wrong person. That counts as causing the loss by hand.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who offers this new explanation
Collateral, a pledge held to guarantee a debt
And he took it from him

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows what 'doing it by hand' means: the judge physically moves the money or item, not just speaks a ruling.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
For example, where he had collateral in his hand,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the one with the claim, holding the other side's item as a pledge for the debt.

phrases.english: and the judge took it from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רבינא אמר: כגון שהיה לו בידו משכון
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 6 rejects the earlier reading, רבינא answers in a different way.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines a case that fits the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A judge who wrongly exempts someone only spoke, so he did not cause the loss with his hands.
steps.terutzMaskana: If he took collateral from the lender and handed it over, he caused the loss physically.

steps.title: Purity cases: touching a שרץ and mixing produce
steps.stepSummary: The same idea applies to purity rulings. A judge who called a pure item impure made it touch a שרץ. A judge who called an impure item pure mixed it in with the owner's pure produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He declared the pure impure': where he made a שרץ touch it. 'He declared the impure pure': where he mixed it in with his produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the purity cases from the משנה in בכורות, showing how the judge caused the loss with his own hands in each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'this is impure' alone does not damage anything. Here the judge actually touched a pure item to a שרץ and so made it impure. Calling impure food 'pure' and then mixing it into the owner's pure produce spreads the טומאה and ruins all of it.

keyTerms.meaning: He declared a pure item impure
He declared an impure item pure
A creeping creature whose dead body makes things impure
That he mixed them together

steps.whatToRemember: In each case the judge causes the loss with a physical act: taking the collateral, touching the item to a שרץ, or mixing impure produce into pure produce.

phrases.english: He declared the pure impure:
phrases.notes: This quotes a case from the משנה in בכורות about a judge who ruled wrongly.

phrases.english: where he made a creeping creature touch it.
He declared the impure pure:
where he mixed them among his produce.

steps.triggerLanguage: טימא את הטהור, דאגע ביה שרץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same 'by hand' idea from step 7 to the purity cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines cases that fit the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A wrong purity ruling is only words, so the judge did not cause the loss himself.
steps.terutzMaskana: The judge did a physical act (touching to a שרץ, mixing the produce) that caused the loss.

steps.title: A convicted person is brought back if someone has a reason to acquit him
steps.stepSummary: Returning to the משנה on דיני נפשות, a ברייתא learns from 'נקי אל תהרג' that a person leaving court convicted is brought back if someone offers a reason to acquit him.
steps.simpleTranslation: About the משנה's words 'capital cases': the רבנן taught that if a person is leaving court after being found guilty, and someone says 'I can argue for his innocence', we bring him back. We learn this from the פסוק 'Do not kill the innocent'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה about דיני נפשות and brings a ברייתא that gives the source for reopening a case to acquit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person was already found guilty, but he may really be נקי, innocent. Because the Torah says not to kill an innocent person, the court must hear any new argument that could save him, even after the verdict.

keyTerms.meaning: Capital cases, where a life is at stake
The Rabbis taught; it opens a ברייתא
A reason to acquit
They bring him back to court
Innocent, someone who may not truly be guilty

phrases.english: Capital cases, etc.
The Rabbis taught:
From where do we know, about one who is leaving court found liable,
and someone said
"I have a reason to teach in his favor,"
from where do we know that they bring him back?
The verse says: "The innocent you shall not kill."

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת כּוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מִנַּיִין לְיוֹצֵא מִבֵּית דִּין חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section, going back to the משנה after the discussion of a judge's mistakes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person leaving court convicted is brought back if someone offers a reason to acquit him, based on 'נקי אל תהרג'.

steps.title: An acquitted person is not brought back to be convicted
steps.stepSummary: The second half of the ברייתא learns from 'צדיק אל תהרג' that a person who was acquitted is not brought back, even if someone has a new argument against him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person is leaving court after being found not guilty, and someone says 'I can argue that he is guilty', we do not bring him back. We learn this from 'Do not kill the righteous'.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes its teaching with the opposite case: once a person is acquitted, the court does not reopen the case against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court already declared this man צדיק, righteous. Once that happens the case stays closed, and a new argument for guilt is not heard. The two halves of the same פסוק give the two halves of the משנה's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Acquitted, found not guilty
A reason to convict
Righteous; here, someone the court already declared innocent

steps.whatToRemember: In דיני נפשות a case is reopened to acquit (נקי אל תהרג) but never reopened to convict (צדיק אל תהרג).

phrases.english: And from where do we know, about one who is leaving court acquitted,
and someone said:
"I have a reason to teach against him,"
from where do we know that they do not bring him back?
The verse says: "The righteous you shall not kill."
phrases.notes: This is the second half of the same פסוק, שמות 23:7.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִנַּיִין לְיוֹצֵא מִבֵּית דִּין זַכַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא with the opposite case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An acquitted person is not brought back for a new argument to convict, based on 'צדיק אל תהרג'.

steps.title: For a מסית the rule is reversed
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר אשי says that for a מסית, someone who leads others to idol worship, the rule is the opposite, based on 'לא תחמל ולא תכסה עליו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר אשי said: for a מסית it is the other way around, because the Torah says 'Do not pity him and do not cover up for him'.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי בר אשי adds an exception: with a מסית, the special mercy we just learned does not apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah tells us not to pity or protect a מסית. So we do not bring him back to acquit him, and if he was acquitted we do bring him back to convict him. It is still a capital case, but the retrial rules run in reverse.

keyTerms.meaning: The opposite, the reverse
A person who persuades others to worship idols
Do not have pity
Do not cover up, do not protect him

steps.confusionAlert: 'The opposite' means both halves flip: for a מסית we reopen to convict, and we do not reopen to acquit.

phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ashi said:
And the opposite applies to a מסית,
as it is written: "Do not pity, and do not cover up for him."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי: וְחִילּוּפָא לְמֵסִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an exception case where the ברייתא's rule is reversed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a מסית, the court reopens a case to convict but not to acquit.

steps.title: רב כהנא learns the מסית rule from a different פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא teaches the same reverse rule for a מסית, but learns it from 'כי הרג תהרגנו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא taught the same idea using a different פסוק: 'You shall surely kill him'.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא gives a different source for the same rule about a מסית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling does not change, only the source does. רב כהנא uses the doubled word 'הרג תהרגנו', which shows the Torah's strictness with a מסית, in place of 'לא תחמל ולא תכסה'.

keyTerms.meaning: Teaches it, gives the teaching
You shall surely kill him

phrases.english: Rav Kahana teaches it
from: "But you shall surely kill him."
phrases.notes: דברים 13:10. He means the same rule about a מסית, just learned from this פסוק.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא מַתְנֵי מִ״כִּי הָרֹג תַּהַרְגֶנּוּ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another source for the ruling in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The reverse retrial rule for a מסית is learned from 'כי הרג תהרגנו'.

steps.title: רבי זירא asks about people liable to exile
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא asks רב ששת where we learn that the same retrial rules apply to חייבי גלות, people who killed by accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא asked רב ששת: where do we learn this for people who must go into exile?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up the next move: רבי זירא asks for a source that extends the rule to cases of accidental killing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק 'נקי וצדיק אל תהרג' talks about killing, so it fits a case where the punishment is death. Someone who killed by accident is sent to a city of refuge, not killed, so רבי זירא wants to know how the same rules reach him.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him
People who must go to exile in a city of refuge for killing by accident

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִנֵּיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira asked Rav Sheshet:
Those liable to exile, from where do we know?
phrases.notes: He means: from where do we know they follow the same rules about bringing the case back?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִנֵּיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת: חַיָּיבֵי גָּלִיּוֹת מִנַּיִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks whether the retrial rules reach a case that is not punished by death.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that חייבי גלות follow the same retrial rules as capital cases.

steps.title: Learned from the word 'רוצח' appearing in both places
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers with a גזירה שוה: the word 'רוצח' is used for both the deliberate killer and the accidental killer, so the rules carry over.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes from 'murderer' and 'murderer': the same word appears in both places.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers that the Torah uses the same word, 'רוצח', for both kinds of killer, and this links their laws.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a גזירה שוה, learning from a shared word. Because the accidental killer is also called 'רוצח', he is treated like the deliberate killer here: his case is reopened to clear him but not to convict him.

keyTerms.meaning: It is learned, it comes from
A killer
Learning one law from another because the Torah uses the same word in both

steps.whatToRemember: The retrial rules of a capital case also apply to חייבי גלות, through the shared word 'רוצח'.

phrases.english: It is learned from "murderer" and "murderer."
phrases.notes: The word appears for the deliberate killer and for the accidental killer, see במדבר 35.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָתְיָא ״רֹצֵחַ״ ״רֹצֵחַ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי זירא's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה from the word 'רוצח', which is used for both the deliberate killer and the accidental killer.

steps.title: Where do we learn the same rules for people who get lashes?
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא continues his question to רב ששת: where do we learn that people liable for מלקות follow the same retrial rules?
steps.simpleTranslation: And people who are liable for lashes, where do we learn it from?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא asks a second question, right after the one about accidental killers. Now he wants a source for people who get lashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The retrial rules were taught for capital cases. Step 14 extended them to חייבי גלות. Now רבי זירא asks whether they also apply to cases of מלקות, which are not death-penalty cases.

keyTerms.meaning: People who are liable to receive lashes
From where do we learn it?

phrases.english: Those liable for lashes, from where do we learn it?
phrases.notes: He means: where do we learn that the retrial rules of capital cases apply to them too?

steps.triggerLanguage: חַיָּיבֵי מַלְקִיּוֹת מִנַּיִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second part of רבי זירא's question, parallel to the question about חייבי גלות
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that people liable for מלקות follow the same retrial rules as capital cases

steps.title: It comes from the word 'wicked' in both places
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers with a גזירה שוה: the word 'רשע' is used for the murderer and for the one who gets lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is learned from 'wicked' and 'wicked'.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers that the Torah calls both the murderer and the person who gets lashes a 'רשע', so the rules carry over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like 'רוצח' linked the accidental killer to the murderer, the shared word 'רשע' links the person who gets lashes to the murderer. Because of that link, the same retrial rules apply in cases of מלקות.

keyTerms.meaning: It comes, meaning it is learned
Wicked person; the shared word that creates the link

phrases.english: It is learned from 'wicked' and 'wicked'.
phrases.notes: The murderer is called רשע in במדבר 35:31, and the one who gets lashes in דברים 25:2.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָתְיָא ״רָשָׁע״ ״רָשָׁע״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה from the word 'רשע' links מלקות cases to capital cases

steps.title: A ברייתא teaches both of these sources
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says exactly what רב ששת said, for both exile and lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא: Those liable for exile, where do we learn it? It is learned from 'murderer' and 'murderer'. Those liable for lashes, where do we learn it? It is learned from 'wicked' and 'wicked'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רב ששת's two answers are also found in a ברייתא. This supports what he said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is added to the law here. The ברייתא repeats both links, 'רוצח' for exile and 'רשע' for lashes, which shows that רב ששת's answers match an earlier teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא
People liable to go into exile for killing by accident
Killer; the word shared by the deliberate and the accidental killer

phrases.english: It is also taught this way:
Those liable for exile, where do we learn it?
It is learned from 'murderer' and 'murderer'.
Those liable for lashes, where do we learn it?
It is learned from 'wicked' and 'wicked'.

steps.whatToRemember: The retrial rules of capital cases also apply to accidental killers (from 'רוצח') and to people who get lashes (from 'רשע').
steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא נָמֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב ששת's answers from steps 14 and 16 with a ברייתא
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with the same two derivations

steps.title: The 'no retrial to convict' rule only covers some mistakes
steps.stepSummary: Quoting the משנה, רבי יוחנן says the acquittal stands only if the judges erred in something the צדוקים do not accept. A mistake in an open Torah law is reversed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And we do not bring him back to convict him.' רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: This is only when the judge made a mistake in something the צדוקים do not agree to. But if he made a mistake in something the צדוקים do agree to, that is something you could go learn in a children's school.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה's rule that an acquitted person is not brought back to be convicted. רבי יוחנן limits that rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The צדוקים only accepted what is written openly in the Torah. A mistake in something they reject, which is known from tradition, leaves the acquittal standing. A mistake in a clear written law is so basic, like a schoolchild's mistake, that the ruling is not a real judgment, so it is reversed even if that leads to a conviction.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not bring him back to be convicted
צדוקים, a group that accepted only the written Torah
Agree to it
Go read it in the children's school; something basic

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוחנן is not cancelling the משנה. The acquittal still stands for most mistakes. Only a clear mistake in a written Torah law is reversed.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the line between a judge's mistake that cannot be undone and one so basic that the ruling does not count.

phrases.english: And we do not bring him back to convict.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
This is only when he made a mistake in a matter
that the Sadducees do not agree to,
but if he made a mistake in a matter
that the Sadducees do agree to,
it is something you could go learn in school.
phrases.notes: He means it is so basic a child knows it, so this kind of mistake gets reversed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין מַחְזִירִין לְחוֹבָה. אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic by quoting a new phrase from the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An acquittal stands only if the error was in a matter the צדוקים reject. An error in an open Torah law is reversed.

steps.title: What about a mistake regarding a man and woman who committed adultery?
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא asks רבי יוחנן what happens if the judge made a mistake about a נואף and נואפת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא asked רבי יוחנן: If the judge made a mistake about a man and woman who committed adultery, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא בר אבא tests the new rule on a specific case. He asks if a mistake about adultery counts as a clear Torah mistake that gets reversed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is which side of רבי יוחנן's line this case falls on. Is it a written law that even the צדוקים accept, so the ruling is reversed, or not?

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him
A man and a woman who commit adultery
What is the law?

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba asked Rabbi Yochanan:
If he made a mistake about an adulterer and adulteress, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבי יוחנן's rule from step 18 to a specific case
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a mistake about adultery is reversed like a clear Torah mistake

steps.title: Use the moment: add this case to the rule
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers with a saying: while your fire is burning, cut your squash and roast it. He means this case fits the rule he just taught.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: While your fire is burning, go cut your squash and roast it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers with a picture: use the fire while it is still hot. He means: add this case to the rule I just gave you.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying tells the student to grab the chance while the topic is fresh. The answer is that a mistake about adultery is like a clear Torah mistake, so it is reversed, as step 21 states openly.

keyTerms.meaning: While your fire is burning
Cut your squash and roast it

phrases.english: He said to him:
While your fire is burning,
go cut your squash and roast it.
phrases.notes: A saying that means: use the chance now and add this case to the rule I just taught.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַדְּמוֹקְדָךְ יְקִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי חייא בר אבא's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The adultery case belongs under the rule: it is a clear Torah mistake, so the ruling is reversed

steps.title: It was stated openly: a mistake about adultery is reversed
steps.stepSummary: Another report from רבי יוחנן, through רבי אמי, says it plainly: if the judge erred about a נואף, the case comes back.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also stated: רבי אמי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: If he made a mistake about an adulterer, the ruling is reversed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second report of רבי יוחנן's teaching. It states plainly what the saying in step 20 hinted at.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 answered with a picture, and this report gives the clear ruling: a mistake about a נואף is reversed. This confirms that it counts as a basic Torah mistake, which does not fall under the משנה's 'no retrial to convict' rule.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also stated (another report of a teaching)
It goes back; the ruling is reversed

steps.whatToRemember: An acquittal normally stands. But if the judges erred in a clear written Torah law, such as the law of a נואף, the ruling is reversed.

phrases.english: It was also stated:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ami said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
If he made a mistake about an adulterer, the ruling is reversed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר נָמֵי, אָמַר רַבִּי אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Confirms and states plainly the answer hinted at in step 20
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A judge's mistake about a נואף is a clear Torah mistake, so the ruling is reversed.

steps.title: So when does the acquittal stand?
steps.stepSummary: Since a mistake about a נואף is reversed, the גמרא asks what kind of mistake would let the acquittal stand.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what is the case where they do not go back?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It asks for an example of a mistake where the acquittal is NOT reversed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last step said that even an error about a נואף brings the case back. That seems to cover a lot of cases. So the גמרא wants to know what is left for the rule that an acquittal stands.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How does it look?
They do not go back (the acquittal is not reversed)

phrases.english: Rather, what is the case
where they do not go back?
phrases.notes: He means the case where the acquittal stays, even though the judge made a mistake.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הֵיכִי דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from step 21: if a mistake about a נואף is reversed, what mistake is not?
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete case where a judge's mistaken acquittal is not reversed.

steps.title: A mistake about relations done in an unusual way
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, through רבי אבהו, says the acquittal stands when the judge erred about relations שלא כדרכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי יוחנן: for example, where he made a mistake about relations done in an unusual way.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives the example: the judge acquitted because he thought relations done in an unusual way do not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits the rule from step 18. The acquittal is reversed only for a mistake in an open, clear Torah law. That relations שלא כדרכה count is not openly stated in a פסוק, so a mistake about it is not reversed.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who reports רבי יוחנן's answer
Not in the usual way (relations done in an unusual manner)

steps.whatToRemember: A mistake in an open Torah law brings the case back. A mistake in a law that is not openly written, like relations שלא כדרכה, lets the acquittal stand.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
For example, where he erred about relations in an unusual way.
phrases.notes: The judge thought this kind of relations doesn't count, so he acquitted the man.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The acquittal stands when the judge erred about relations שלא כדרכה, a law not openly written in the Torah.

steps.title: Does 'everyone' include the witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that 'everyone' may argue, and asks if this includes the witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'In money cases, everyone, etc.' Everyone, even the witnesses?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic from the משנה. It asks whether 'everyone' who may argue for acquittal in a capital case includes the witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that in capital cases everyone may argue for acquittal. The word 'everyone' sounds like it covers every person there, even the witnesses. The גמרא asks whether that is really meant.

keyTerms.meaning: Money cases
Everyone
Witnesses

phrases.english: In money cases, everyone, etc.
phrases.notes: The משנה goes on: in capital cases, everyone may argue for acquittal, but not everyone may argue for guilt. The question is about that part.

phrases.english: Everyone, and even witnesses?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַכֹּל, וַאֲפִילּוּ עֵדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the word 'everyone' in the משנה includes the witnesses.

steps.title: Does the משנה follow only a minority view?
steps.stepSummary: If witnesses are included, the משנה would follow רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה and not the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say our משנה follows רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה, and not the רבנן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests that if witnesses may argue for acquittal, then the משנה matches only one תנא. The proof comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually we do not want a plain משנה to follow a lone view against the רבנן. So this suggestion puts pressure on reading 'everyone' as including witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (a suggestion the גמרא may later reject)
A תנא, son of רבי יהודה
The Sages (the main group view)

phrases.english: Shall we say our משנה
is the view of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda,
and not the Rabbis?

steps.triggerLanguage: נֵימָא מַתְנִיתִין רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws out the result of reading 'everyone' as including witnesses.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain reading of the משנה that 'everyone' includes witnesses.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If witnesses are included, the משנה follows a minority view against the רבנן.

steps.title: The ברייתא about a witness speaking
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that the רבנן say a witness may not argue at all, while רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה lets him argue for acquittal.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'One witness shall not answer against a person,' neither for acquittal nor for guilt. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה says: he may answer for acquittal, but not for guilt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show the two views behind its suggestion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן learn from the פסוק that a witness may not add any argument, for either side. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה allows a witness to argue for acquittal. So a משנה letting witnesses argue for acquittal would match only him.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
Answers, speaks up
For acquittal, in his favor
For guilt, against him

phrases.english: As it was taught:
"But one witness shall not answer against a person" –
whether for acquittal or for guilt.
phrases.notes: This first part is the view of the רבנן.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, says:
He may answer for acquittal,
but he may not answer for guilt.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the suggestion in step 25.
steps.raayaObject: That letting witnesses argue for acquittal is only the view of רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on the פסוק 'ועד אחד לא יענה בנפש'.

steps.title: 'Everyone' means one of the students
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the משנה means one of the students, not the witnesses, so it fits everyone's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: it means one of the students, and so it is the view of all.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא rejects the suggestion. He explains that 'everyone' in the משנה refers to the students sitting before the court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'everyone' means the students and not the witnesses, the משנה says nothing about witnesses. Then even the רבנן can agree to it, and it does not follow only רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who answers
Students (who sat before the court)
The view of all, everyone agrees

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's 'everyone may argue for acquittal' means the students, not the witnesses. So the משנה fits both the רבנן and רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה.
steps.confusionAlert: The word הכל shows up twice with different meanings. In the משנה it means 'everyone' at the trial. In דברי הכל it means 'all the תנאים agree.'

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
It means one of the students,
and so it is the view of all.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: בְּאֶחָד מִן הַתַּלְמִידִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 25 by reading 'everyone' differently.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the משנה follows only רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The suggestion assumed 'everyone' includes witnesses, but it means the students.
